note.note:
Action Plan:
1. Localized reaction to recent insect sting (right arm): advised immediate use of an oral antihistamine (e.g., Piriton / chlorphenamine 4 mg, dose/route/frequency: one tablet up to six times daily, or a once-daily non-sedating alternative); observe the sting site for spreading erythema, heat, or signs of infection; return or call emergency services urgently if lip/tongue swelling, stridor, or breathing difficulty develops.  
2. Education and written/online information link provided on recognition of anaphylaxis and when to attend ED.  
3. No allergy testing indicated at this time; consider if reactions become recurrent.  
4. Safety-net advice: lower threshold to contact GP for any worsening or new concerns.  
5. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Reason for visit: difficulty breathing, mild lip tingling/swelling, and rash at sting site minutes after bee/wasp sting.  
• Onset: a “few minutes ago.”  
• Course: symptoms stable during video call; anxiety regarding possible deterioration.  
• Past medical history: eczema; occasional anxiety (no pharmacotherapy).  
• Allergies: penicillin.  
• Medications: none; has not taken antihistamine yet.  
• Social: 27-year-old male, computer scientist, lives alone with a cat.

Objective:
Telemedicine examination  
• General: alert, speaking full sentences without distress.  
• Respiratory: no visible or audible respiratory compromise; no stridor.  
• Oropharynx: no intra-oral or lip swelling noted; airway patent.  
• Dermatologic: small puncture mark with mild erythema, no visible swelling, on right arm.  
• Vitals: not available (remote consultation).

Assessment & Plan:

1. Localized allergic reaction to insect sting  
   - Assessment: Localized allergic reaction (stage 1); no current signs of systemic anaphylaxis.  
   - Differential diagnosis: evolving systemic allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), local cellulitis (if erythema/heat spreads).  
   - Investigations: none required now; consider blood allergy testing if reactions recur.  
   - Treatment: Oral antihistamine (chlorphenamine 4 mg up to six times daily or a once-daily non-sedating agent), PRN. Provide patient education sheet on anaphylaxis. Consider oral antibiotics if sting site becomes hot, painful, or erythema spreads (not indicated presently).  
   - Referrals: none at present; ED if acute deterioration.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: baseline vitals could not be obtained via video; full medication reconciliation limited to patient report.  
● Internal conflicts: none identified.  
● Transcript quality: clear audio; minor conversational fillers removed.
